rv.q: But the evening doesn’t overwhelm you as it could, partly because the build-up feels rather sticky, and partly because the play makes immense demands of the central character and Thandie Newton doesn’t find the depth she needs.
But, while it makes a taut evening and the issues are as relevant as ever, Dorfman's chosen form now looks a little too neat.
The poverty of his lead actor makes a beautifully constructed psychological thriller surprisingly hard work to watch.
But her voice is severely limited in range and colour and her emotional register underwhelming.

This is a production which manages to manipulate our sympathies and if it doesn't quite pulsate with the terrifying emotional intensity that I remember from the original, the play is a fitting opener for the newly-renamed Harold Pinter Theatre - powerful, unsettling, ambiguous and refusing to give any neat answers.
The poverty of his lead actor makes a beautifully constructed psychological thriller, if not exactly torture, surprisingly hard work to watch.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this moral thriller, with critics finding it a taut evening that raises powerful questions about justice and revenge, though Newton's performance divides opinion and some feel the production lacks full impact.
